Getting started

Source: vignettes/getting-started.Rmd
getting-started.Rmd

spigot lets you build a Shiny app the way you would build a small website: pages are hand-written HTML and JavaScript, and the server side is a set of plumber endpoints. spigot mounts the plumber router inside the Shiny app, so the pages and the API share one process, one origin and one port. Shiny still hosts the app (locally, on Shiny Server or on Posit Connect), gives each browser tab a session, and keeps a websocket open to it.

Browser tab ──HTTP fetch──▶ /api/*  ──▶ plumber router ─┐
     ▲                                                  │ same R process,
     │                                                  │ same memory
     └──websocket (Shiny session)◀── observers/push ◀───┘

The API is for the app’s own pages, not for other clients. By default it answers only requests that carry the session token of an open tab of the app.

This vignette walks through two of the examples that ship with spigot: minimal, one page and four endpoints, and site, a three-page site with shared templates and an endpoint that runs its work in another process. vignette("reactivity", package = "spigot") covers the third example, live, and pushing data to pages.

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("kent-orr/spigot")

Run any example with run_example():

spigot::run_example("minimal")

The minimal example

An app is a folder with an app.R. The minimal example’s folder holds:

minimal/
├── app.R        # spigot_app(): the page and the API
├── api.R        # plumber endpoints, served under /api
├── index.html   # the page
└── www/         # files served as they are
    ├── app.js
    └── style.css

app.R 

# spigot "minimal" example: one hand-written page calling a plumber API that
# runs inside this Shiny app, on the same origin and port.
#
# Run it with spigot::run_example("minimal").
library(spigot)

spigot_app(
  # A full HTML document. spigot adds Shiny's scripts and spigot.js to its
  # <head>.
  pages = spigot_page("index.html"),
  # The API is a plain plumber file, served under /api.
  api = "api.R"
)

spigot_app() returns an ordinary Shiny app object, so shiny::runApp("minimal"), Shiny Server and Posit Connect all run the folder like any other app (see Running the app). Its arguments:

  • pages: one page, served at /, or a named list of pages keyed by path.
  • api: a plumber file, or a router you built in code with spigot_api().
  • prefix: where the API is mounted; "/api" by default.
  • server: an optional Shiny server function, for push and reactivity.
  • require_session: TRUE by default; see Sessions below.

Running the app

Run the app’s folder:

shiny::runApp("minimal")   # or shiny::runApp("minimal/app.R")

RStudio’s Run App button, Shiny Server, Posit Connect and run_example() do the same. Shiny loads any .R files in the folder’s R/ subfolder, sources app.R from inside the folder, serves www/, and keeps the folder as the working directory while the app runs.

Running the app object is different. Printing the object spigot_app() returns runs it, and that happens at the console, when app.R is sourced with echo, and with Rscript app.R. Shiny then does none of the above:

runApp("minimal") the printed object
spigot_page("index.html"), api = "api.R" read from the folder read from the working directory, an error if they are not there
files in www/ served 404
functions in R/ loaded not loaded

So a page’s <script src="app.js"> gets spigot’s HTML 404 page, which the browser refuses to run (“blocked due to MIME type”), and an endpoint that calls a function from R/ fails with a 500. From a terminal, use Rscript -e 'shiny::runApp("minimal")'. An app that keeps its page and API in one script, like the one in the README, reads no files and runs either way.

api.R: the endpoints

api.R is a plain plumber file. Annotate a function with #* @get /path (or @post, @put, @delete), and its arguments come from the query string and the JSON body.

# The example's API. Ordinary plumber annotations; spigot mounts the router at
# /api and serialises results with spigot_json().

#* Greet someone. A GET with a query parameter.
#* @get /hello
function(name = "world") {
  list(message = sprintf("Hello, %s!", name), at = Sys.time())
}

#* Echo a JSON body back. Shows request parsing and response serialisation.
#* @post /echo
function(req) {
  list(received = req$body, received_at = Sys.time())
}

#* Summarise n random normal draws. A data frame becomes an array of row
#* objects; bad input gets a 400 with a JSON error.
#* @get /summary
function(res, n = "1000") {
  n <- suppressWarnings(as.integer(n))
  if (is.na(n) || n < 1 || n > 1e5) {
    res$status <- 400L
    return(list(error = "n must be a whole number from 1 to 100000"))
  }
  x <- stats::rnorm(n)
  p <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)
  list(
    n = n,
    mean = mean(x),
    sd = stats::sd(x),
    quantiles = data.frame(p = p, value = unname(stats::quantile(x, p)))
  )
}

#* Wait, then answer, without blocking the R process: the endpoint returns a
#* promise that a later() timer resolves. Other requests are served meanwhile.
#* (For real work in another process, use promises::future_promise().)
#* @get /slow
function(seconds = "2") {
  secs <- min(max(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(seconds)), 0.1, na.rm = TRUE), 10)
  started <- Sys.time()
  promises::promise(function(resolve, reject) {
    later::later(function() {
      resolve(list(waited = secs, started = started, finished = Sys.time()))
    }, delay = secs)
  })
}

Replies are JSON, serialised by spigot_json(): length-1 vectors become scalars, NA becomes null, and a data frame becomes an array of row objects. Wrap a value in I() to keep a length-1 vector as an array. Setting res$status sends another status code, and the page’s code can read the JSON body of the error.

Request bodies are parsed by plumber as usual: JSON, forms and multipart uploads. For a binary body, such as a file sent as a Blob, give the endpoint #* @parser octet; plumber’s default parsers would try to read it as text.

index.html: the page

spigot_page("index.html") reads a complete HTML document. spigot adds jQuery, Shiny’s JavaScript and spigot.js to its <head> when it serves the page, so the template needs no script tags for them. It needs only a </head> tag, and loads its own files from www/ with relative URLs (style.css, app.js).

The template is a whisker (Mustache) template; data fills it in. The minimal page has no {{ }} tags; the site example below uses them.

www/app.js: calling the API

spigot.js defines spigot.get(), spigot.post(), spigot.put() and spigot.del(). Paths are relative to the API, so spigot.get("hello", {name: "Ada"}) requests api/hello?name=Ada relative to the page, which keeps working when the app is served under a subpath. Each call returns a promise of the parsed JSON reply:

const reply = await spigot.get("hello", { name: "Ada" });
reply.message;   // "Hello, Ada!"

try {
  await spigot.get("summary", { n: 0 });
} catch (err) {
  // A non-2xx reply, or no reply at all (err.status is then 0).
  err.status;    // 400
  err.message;   // "n must be a whole number from 1 to 100000": the JSON `error` field
  err.body;      // the whole parsed reply
}

The example’s page script wraps these calls to show each outcome:

// The page's only script. It calls the mounted API with spigot.js, which
// spigot_app() adds to every page: spigot.get() and spigot.post() take paths
// relative to the API ("hello" means api/hello, relative to this page, so the
// app also works under a subpath on Shiny Server or Posit Connect), send this
// tab's Shiny session token, and wait for the session if it has not started.
// They resolve with the parsed JSON reply and reject with a SpigotError
// ({status, message, body}) for any non-2xx reply.

// Run one call and describe the outcome for show().
async function call(label, promise) {
  const t0 = performance.now();
  const ms = () => Math.round(performance.now() - t0);
  try {
    const data = await promise;
    return { label, ok: true, outcome: "OK", ms: ms(), data };
  } catch (err) {
    if (!(err instanceof spigot.SpigotError)) throw err;
    // status 0 means no reply: a timeout or a network failure.
    const outcome = err.status ? String(err.status) : "no reply";
    return { label, ok: false, outcome, ms: ms(), data: err.body ?? err.message };
  }
}

function show(el, r) {
  el.textContent = `${r.label}  →  ${r.outcome}  (${r.ms} ms)\n\n` +
    (typeof r.data === "string" ? r.data : JSON.stringify(r.data, null, 2));
  el.classList.toggle("err", !r.ok);
}

function showError(el, err) {
  el.textContent = err.message;
  el.classList.add("err");
}

const $ = (id) => document.getElementById(id);

$("hello-form").addEventListener("submit", async (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  const name = $("hello-name").value;
  show($("hello-out"), await call("GET api/hello", spigot.get("hello", { name })));
});

$("echo-form").addEventListener("submit", async (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  const out = $("echo-out");
  let body;
  try { body = JSON.parse($("echo-body").value); }
  catch (err) { showError(out, new Error("the box does not hold valid JSON")); return; }
  show(out, await call("POST api/echo", spigot.post("echo", body)));
});

$("summary-form").addEventListener("submit", async (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  const n = $("summary-n").value;
  show($("summary-out"), await call("GET api/summary", spigot.get("summary", { n })));
});

// The async demo appends to a running log.
const slowLog = [];
function logLine(line) {
  slowLog.push(`${new Date().toLocaleTimeString()}  ${line}`);
  $("slow-out").textContent = slowLog.slice(-12).join("\n");
  $("slow-out").classList.remove("err");
}

$("slow-btn").addEventListener("click", async () => {
  logLine("slow: sent, waiting 3 s ...");
  const r = await call("slow", spigot.get("slow", { seconds: 3 }));
  logLine(`slow: ${r.outcome} after ${r.ms} ms`);
});

$("ping-btn").addEventListener("click", async () => {
  const r = await call("ping", spigot.get("hello", { name: "ping" }));
  logLine(`ping: ${r.outcome} after ${r.ms} ms`);
});

vignette("client", package = "spigot") documents the whole client.

Sessions

Each browser tab is a Shiny session. spigot.js waits for it to start, then sends its token with every request in an X-Spigot-Session header, and spigot binds the request to that session. An endpoint gets the session with spigot_session(req), and can keep per-tab state in session$userData:

#* @get /visits
function(req) {
  s <- spigot::spigot_session(req)
  s$userData$visits <- sum(s$userData$visits, 1)
  list(visits = s$userData$visits)
}

With require_session = TRUE, the default, a request without the token of an open tab gets a 401, so curl and other sites cannot call the API. Use require_session = FALSE for an API that should also answer those requests; spigot_session() then returns NULL for them. Whatever the setting, requests from pages on another origin get a 403.

The site example

site is a small site about R’s mtcars data with three pages: a home page, a table of the cars, and a page that fits a regression. It shows templates with data, shared partials, blueprints, and an endpoint whose work runs in another R process.

site/
├── app.R
├── api.R
├── R/                  # loaded by Shiny before app.R
│   ├── data.R          # the data, and a page() helper
│   ├── pages-cars.R    # the cars blueprint
│   └── pages-model.R   # the model blueprint
├── templates/
│   ├── index.html
│   ├── partials/       # shared by every page
│   │   ├── head.html
│   │   ├── nav.html
│   │   └── footer.html
│   ├── cars/cars.html
│   └── model/model.html
└── static/
    ├── site.css
    ├── cars/cars.js
    └── model/model.js
# spigot "site" example: a small multi-page site about R's mtcars data.
#
# * Templates live in templates/, shared partials (the <head>, the nav bar and
#   the footer) in templates/partials/, and files the pages load in static/.
# * The /cars and /model sections are blueprints, defined in R/: each has its
#   own templates and static files. Shiny loads R/ before this file.
# * The /cars page is rendered in R with every row; its filter form then
#   calls the API and redraws the table in the browser.
# * The /model page calls an endpoint that bootstraps a regression in a
#   future worker, another R process, so the app keeps serving other tabs.
#
# Run it with spigot::run_example("site"). It needs the future package.
library(spigot)

# The fit endpoint hands its work to background R processes.
future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 2)
shiny::onStop(function() future::plan(future::sequential))

spigot_app(
  pages = list(
    "/" = page("index.html", "home", "Home", list(
      n = nrow(car_data),
      predictors = length(predictors)
    ))
  ),
  blueprints = list("/cars" = cars, "/model" = model),
  api = "api.R",
  templates = "templates",
  partials = "templates/partials",
  static = "static"
)

templates, partials and static say where the files are; the /cars and /model sections are blueprints, each with its own templates and static files:

# The cars section: its page renders every row in R; static/cars/cars.js
# filters them through the API. Mounted at /cars in app.R.
cars <- spigot::spigot_blueprint(
  pages = page("cars.html", "cars", "Cars", list(
    rows = unname(whisker::rowSplit(car_data[c("model", "mpg", "cyl", "hp", "wt")]))
  )),
  templates = "templates/cars",
  static = "static/cars"
)

vignette("flask-flow", package = "spigot") explains this layout.

Several pages

pages is a named list keyed by path. A request for /cars/ is redirected to /cars, and a path that is neither a page nor a static file gets a 404 page. Pages can also be nested ("/docs/intro"); see ?spigot_page for how their relative URLs resolve.

A top-level page can also be any Shiny UI, such as a fluidPage(), so a classic Shiny page can sit next to hand-written ones.

Templates, data and partials

Each page’s data is a list for its template. {{title}} inserts a value with HTML escaped, so data can never inject markup or R code, {{#rows}} ... {{/rows}} repeats for each element of a list, and {{> nav}} inserts a partial. Here is the cars page, which R renders with all 32 rows:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
{{> head}}
<body>
  {{> nav}}
  <main>
    <h1>Cars</h1>
    <form id="filter" class="row">
      <label>Model contains <input id="q" autocomplete="off" placeholder="e.g. merc"></label>
      <label>At least <input id="min_mpg" inputmode="decimal" size="4" autocomplete="off"> mpg</label>
      <button type="submit">Filter</button>
      <span class="hint" id="status"></span>
    </form>
    <table id="cars">
      <thead>
        <tr><th>Model</th><th>mpg</th><th>Cylinders</th><th>Horsepower</th><th>Weight</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        {{#rows}}
        <tr data-car="{{model}}"><td>{{model}}</td><td>{{mpg}}</td><td>{{cyl}}</td><td>{{hp}}</td><td>{{wt}}</td></tr>
        {{/rows}}
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </main>
  {{> footer}}
  <script src="{{static}}/cars.js"></script>
</body>
</html>

Its script is <script src="{{static}}/cars.js">: a blueprint’s pages get {{static}}, the path its static files are served at (cars/static).

All three pages share the head, nav and footer partials from templates/partials/. The nav marks the current page with aria-current, using the page value each page’s data sets:

<nav class="site-nav">
  <span class="brand">spigot <span>site example</span></span>
  <!-- Relative links: they keep working when the app runs under a subpath. -->
  <a href="./" data-page="home"{{#page.home}} aria-current="page"{{/page.home}}>Home</a>
  <a href="cars" data-page="cars"{{#page.cars}} aria-current="page"{{/page.cars}}>Cars</a>
  <a href="model" data-page="model"{{#page.model}} aria-current="page"{{/page.model}}>Model</a>
</nav>

data can also be a function of the request, called for each request (for example, to read the query string). The site’s data never changes, so its pages use cache = TRUE and are rendered once.

Server-rendered first, then the API

The cars page arrives with every row already in the HTML. Its filter form then asks the API for the matching rows and redraws the table body, building elements with textContent rather than HTML strings:

// The table arrives rendered in R. Filtering asks the API for matching rows
// and redraws the table body.

const $ = (id) => document.getElementById(id);
const columns = ["model", "mpg", "cyl", "hp", "wt"];

function draw(rows) {
  const body = $("cars").tBodies[0];
  body.replaceChildren(...rows.map((row) => {
    const tr = document.createElement("tr");
    tr.dataset.car = row.model;
    for (const col of columns) {
      const td = document.createElement("td");
      td.textContent = row[col];
      tr.append(td);
    }
    return tr;
  }));
  $("status").textContent = `${rows.length} of 32 cars`;
}

$("filter").addEventListener("submit", async (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  try {
    const reply = await spigot.get("cars", { q: $("q").value, min_mpg: $("min_mpg").value });
    draw(reply.rows);
  } catch (err) {
    if (!(err instanceof spigot.SpigotError)) throw err;
    $("status").textContent = `Error ${err.status}: ${err.message}`;
  }
});

$("status").textContent = `${$("cars").tBodies[0].rows.length} cars`;

Slow work: future_promise()

R runs one thing at a time. While an endpoint runs, the app serves no other request and no other tab, so anything slower than about a tenth of a second should not run in the app’s R process. An endpoint can return a promise instead, and spigot replies when it resolves. The fit endpoint hands its work to a future worker with promises::future_promise():

# The site's API. `car_data` and `predictors` are defined in R/data.R, which
# Shiny loads before app.R; spigot_app() evaluates this file in app.R's
# environment, which sees them.

#* Cars whose model name contains `q` (ignoring case) and that do at least
#* `min_mpg` miles per gallon.
#* @get /cars
function(q = "", min_mpg = "") {
  min_mpg <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(min_mpg))
  if (length(min_mpg) != 1 || is.na(min_mpg)) min_mpg <- -Inf
  keep <- grepl(tolower(q), tolower(car_data$model), fixed = TRUE) & car_data$mpg >= min_mpg
  # A data frame becomes an array of row objects.
  list(rows = car_data[keep, c("model", "mpg", "cyl", "hp", "wt")])
}

#* Regress mpg on one predictor and bootstrap a 95% interval for the slope.
#* The work runs in a future worker, another R process, so this R process
#* keeps serving other requests while it runs.
#* @post /fit
function(res, x = "wt", reps = 1000) {
  if (!is.character(x) || length(x) != 1 || !x %in% names(predictors)) {
    res$status <- 400L
    return(list(error = paste("x must be one of:", paste(names(predictors), collapse = ", "))))
  }
  reps <- suppressWarnings(as.integer(reps))
  if (length(reps) != 1 || is.na(reps) || reps < 100 || reps > 5000) {
    res$status <- 400L
    return(list(error = "reps must be a whole number from 100 to 5000"))
  }

  # Only these values are sent to the worker.
  data <- car_data[c("mpg", x)]
  app_pid <- Sys.getpid()
  promises::future_promise({
    started <- Sys.time()
    slope <- function(d) unname(stats::coef(stats::lm(d$mpg ~ d[[x]]))[2])
    boots <- replicate(reps, slope(data[sample.int(nrow(data), replace = TRUE), ]))
    ci <- unname(stats::quantile(boots, c(0.025, 0.975)))
    list(
      x = x,
      reps = reps,
      slope = list(estimate = slope(data), lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2]),
      seconds = as.numeric(Sys.time() - started, units = "secs"),
      worker_pid = Sys.getpid(),
      app_pid = app_pid
    )
  }, seed = TRUE)
  # The endpoint returns the promise; spigot sends the reply when it resolves.
}

app.R starts the workers with future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 2). The worker is another R process: send it the data it needs, as data is here, and keep sessions, spigot_emit() and other app state in the main process. To push from a worker’s result, do it in the promise’s then(). vignette("reactivity", package = "spigot") has more on this.

Deploying

A spigot app is a Shiny app: deploy its folder as you would any other. Some things to know:

  • Subpaths. Use relative URLs in pages (href="cars", src="logo.png"); spigot.get() and friends already resolve their paths relative to the page. Apps then work under a subpath such as https://example.com/apps/site/.
  • Request size. Shiny rejects request bodies larger than getOption("shiny.maxRequestSize"), 5 MB by default, before any R code runs. That 413 reply is plain text, not JSON. Raise the limit with spigot_app(max_request_size =).
  • Several R processes. Each R process has its own memory and its own sessions. If the server runs several processes for one app (Posit Connect can), state kept in R and spigot_broadcast() reach only the tabs served by the same process.
  • Proxies. The cross-origin check compares the request’s Origin with its Host, or with X-Forwarded-Host when a proxy sets it. A proxy that rewrites Host without setting X-Forwarded-Host makes every POST from the browser fail with 403.
